query: Which material can be used for enhance glass-forming ability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small concentration of zirconium to a base alloy enhances its glass-forming ability by increasing atomic-level packing disorder and frustrating crystallization.
generation.material_initial_state: The base alloy is in a molten state with moderate glass-forming ability.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low concentration (e.g., a few atomic percent) of zirconium into the alloy.
generation.conditions: The alloy is rapidly cooled under controlled conditions; experiments are conducted at similar cooling rates for alloys with and without zirconium.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced atomic-scale packing disorder and local topological frustration mediated by zirconium atoms.
generation.mechanism: Zirconium atoms, due to their relatively large size and chemical affinity, disrupt the regular atomic arrangement of the base alloy, hindering nucleation and growth of crystalline phases during cooling.
generation.predicted_outcome: The zirconium-containing alloy will form a glass (amorphous structure) at a lower critical cooling rate compared to the base alloy without zirconium.
generation.baseline: The base alloy without zirconium addition under identical processing conditions.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold within a specific range of zirconium concentration (likely a few atomic percent) and under rapid cooling conditions; outside these boundaries (e.g., high zirconium content or slow cooling), crystallization may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentration of zirconium and the precise cooling rate threshold remain uncertain without further empirical validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples, one with the base composition and one with the same composition plus a small, controlled amount of zirconium. Process all samples under identical rapid cooling conditions. Characterize the samples using X-ray diffraction and calorimetric analysis to assess the amorphous vs crystalline phase content.
measurements: X-ray diffraction patterns to detect the presence/absence of crystalline peaks
Differential scanning calorimetry to measure the glass transition and crystallization temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the zirconium-added alloy does not exhibit a lower critical cooling rate (i.e., if it does not show a greater tendency to form a glass or if crystallinity is comparable or higher than the control sample), then the hypothesis will be falsified.
